I'm 72 this year. I've been farming these 15 mu since I was 17 — my father taught me, and now my sons help when they're not working in town. I never went to school, but I know this land better than any book ever could. I don't need numbers and formulas to tell me what to do. I watch, I remember, and I talk to the neighbors.

This year I've got 10 mu in wheat and maize, and 5 mu in cotton, same as always. The wheat I put in last October is coming up green now. Winter was dry, so I already gave it one watering when the ground thawed. Now it needs fertilizer before it starts growing fast. I always put down about half a bag of urea per mu when the wheat turns green — that's what my neighbor Old Wang does too, and his wheat always looks strong. Two years ago he tried saving money by skipping the topdress, and his field was thin as straw. Not me. I'll water it two more times before harvest — once at jointing, once at filling. The well water costs money, but without it the yield drops too much. For bugs, I don't spray unless I see them. Last year the aphids came thick on the wheat, so I'll watch close this year.

Cotton goes in the ground in a few days, once the soil warms up. I save some of my own seeds, but I buy new hybrid seeds too — the old ones don't sprout as well after a couple years. One bag of compound fertilizer per mu, spread before planting. Cotton doesn't need as much water as wheat, but I'll irrigate twice — once when it flowers, once when the bolls are forming. Bollworm is the big worry for cotton. If I see them, I spray. No point spraying beforehand and wasting money.

The wheat comes off in early June, and then the real rush starts — we barely have a week to get the maize in. I hire a machine to plow quick, then we plant with the small seeder. Maize is simpler than wheat. I put compound fertilizer in the row at planting, and if the leaves look yellow later, I throw a little urea on top. Two waterings usually, sometimes three if the summer is very dry. We mostly use family labor, but at harvest time I hire a few extra hands — my back isn't what it used to be at 72. My son sends money from his factory job, which helps, but I still don't like spending too much on inputs. I'd rather apply a bit more fertilizer and be safe than risk a bad year. A bad harvest hurts more than saving a few yuan helps.
